hook: The sultan who ruled the Ottoman Empire at its height.

pages.x: Suleiman was born in 1494 in Trabzon, on the Black Sea, the only son of Sultan Selim the Grim. He became sultan in 1520, at 25.
Within a few years he took Belgrade, drove the Knights of St John from the island of Rhodes, and in 1526 crushed the Hungarian army at Mohács, where the young King Louis II drowned as he fled.
In 1529 he besieged Vienna, the heart of Habsburg Europe. Heavy rain, cold and a stubborn defence forced him to turn back. It was the high-water mark of Ottoman power in Europe.

Turks call him Kanuni, "the Lawgiver". He reformed the laws of the empire on land, taxes and crime. His empire stretched from Hungary to Iraq and Algeria, and his navy, under the admiral Barbarossa, ruled the Mediterranean.

He fell in love with Hurrem, an enslaved woman from what is now Ukraine, whom Europeans called Roxelana. Breaking with tradition, he freed and married her, and wrote her love poems. Her power at court became enormous.
His architect, Mimar Sinan, built him the Süleymaniye Mosque on a hill above Istanbul, surrounded by schools, a hospital, kitchens and baths. He and Hurrem are buried beside it.
In 1566, aged 71, he died in his tent while besieging the fortress of Szigetvár in Hungary. His ministers hid his death for weeks so that the army would not lose heart.
Suleiman ruled for 46 years, longer than any other sultan, at the height of Ottoman power. It was a golden age of law, art and architecture, and Europe called him "the Magnificent".
pts: Ruled the Ottoman Empire at its height
Known to Turks as the Lawgiver
Pushed the empire into Hungary and to Vienna's gates
